summary: Annual grants of £350-£5,000 for in-depth research on the history of dress and the materials from which it is made, based on close examination of surviving garments. Within these parameters there are no geographical or chronological restrictions.

title: Beatrice de Cardi Awards
eligibility_summary: From the project director or principal investigator. Not for work contributing to a UG/PG degree; no retrospective applications. Restricted by geography: research must concern the United Arab Emirates, the Sultanate of Oman, Saudi Arabia, or the Pakistan province of Balochistan. Two references required.
summary:
Grants of £5,000-£15,000 for archaeological research (field survey, excavation, and publication) in the UAE, Oman, Saudi Arabia and Balochistan (Pakistan). Post-excavation analysis/publication also eligible for this award only. Renewable annually up to three years.

Beatrice de Cardi undertook pioneering fieldwork and research in the Arabian Gulf and Pakistan. Over the course of a long and distinguished career she was President of the British Foundation for the Study of Arabia, the first Secretary of the Council for British Archaeology, and a recipient of the Society’s Gold Medal. The awards are for the furtherance of archaeological research by field survey, excavation and the publication of the fieldwork in the United Arab Emirates, the Sultanate of Oman, Saudi Arabia, and the Pakistan province of Balochistan.

title: Margaret and Tom Jones Awards
eligibility_summary: From the project director or principal investigator. Not for work contributing to a UG/PG degree; no retrospective applications. Not open to those previously in receipt of funding for Mucking post-excavation. Two references required.
summary:
Grants of £1,000-£10,500 for archaeological investigation, excavation or analysis of large sites or landscapes in the UK (Neolithic to post-Medieval), or the development/testing of methodologies for such work. Renewable annually up to three years.

Between 1965 and 1978 Margaret and Tom Jones oversaw excavation in advance of gravel extraction of an area of 18 hectares overlooking the Thames Estuary at Mucking in Essex. One of the largest and most extensive excavation projects in Europe at the time, this revealed a complex palimpsest of settlement, funerary and landscape features from the Neolithic to the post-Medieval periods. Now published in a five volume report, Mucking remains a key site for UK archaeology and represented a milestone in the development of excavation methods and approaches, and in the archiving, analysis and publication of large and complex archaeological data-sets.

The awards are in memory of Tessa Verney Wheeler (1893 -1936) and Sir Mortimer Wheeler (1890-1976) and were established through an appeal by the British Academy, the Institute of Archaeology (University College London) and the Society of Antiquaries of London.

title: William and Jane Morris Church Conservation Grants
eligibility_summary:
Apply on behalf of a church, chapel or other place of worship in the United Kingdom. Funds conservation of decorative/non-structural interior features (stained glass, sculpture, furniture, monuments/tombs, wall paintings) made no later than 1896. No references required. A professional architect or established conservator must direct the work.

The object must have been made no later than 1896 (the year of William Morris’s death), even if it is in a building which is older. Turret clocks and organs are not grant aided.  However applications for a clock or an organ case that makes a significant contribution to the interior of a church, and/or is of specific antiquarian interest, may exceptionally be considered.
summary:
Grants of £500-£5,000 from the Morris Fund for conservation of decorative or non-structural interior features (pre-1896) in UK places of worship, following SPAB principles. Two application rounds per year.

We make these awards from the Morris Fund, which was formed in 1939 using a bequest to the Society from May Morris, the younger daughter of William and Jane Morris. In accordance with May’s will, we only support work carried out under the principles of the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings (SPAB), which was founded by her father.
notes: Own drop-down on programmes page; application steps on make-a-grant-application page. Two annual rounds: 31 March and 31 August. On 2026-08-21 the 31 Aug 2026 round is still open (2026-08-31 future) -> status=open; both rounds listed (multi_deadline). Applicant is an institution (place of worship), not an individual researcher, but the inclusion rule requires availability to some UK-based researchers only in general; recorded in_scope=yes as it is an open UK research/conservation call. FLAG FOR REVIEW: institutional (place-of-worship) applicant, arguably outside the 'UK-based researchers' intent.

title: The Linda Parry Textile Research and Conservation Grants
amount_raw: up to £4000 per project (page also says 'awards of up to £1000')
eligibility_summary:
Apply on behalf of a church, chapel or other place of worship in the UK and the Crown Dependencies, for research and conservation of textiles. One application per organisation per round. An Icon-accredited conservator must direct the work. Priority to projects of greater historical significance / conservation need; parish churches prioritised over well-funded cathedrals.

The object must have been made no later than 1896 (the year of William Morris’s death), even if it is in a building which is older. We will give priority to applications where the grant will make a significant impact to the viability of the work (either by allowing the work, or unlocking other funding), or where the work is on features of national or international importance.
summary: Grants (up to £4,000 per project) for the research and conservation of textiles in UK/Crown Dependency places of worship. Two application rounds per year; applied for via the Morris Church Conservation Grants form.
